feedback: If a learner says the best genotype should take over and stay, point out that whatever is common becomes the parasites' main target, which hands the advantage back to rare types.
If a learner treats this as hosts adapting to a fixed threat, stress that the parasites themselves are evolving in response — this is reciprocal, not one-sided.
activities.intendedInsight: Fast parasite generations let co-evolutionary cycling be seen on a comprehensible timescale: rare host genotypes gain a temporary edge because parasites are tuned to the common type, so advantage keeps shifting and no genotype wins permanently. This requires standing genetic variation — several genotypes present, one common at a time.
learnerActions: Switch to (or examine) a parasite-host scenario where parasites reproduce much faster than hosts.
Start with a host population containing several genotypes, one of which is initially common, and track their frequencies over many generations.
Observe how parasites adapt to attack the common host type, giving an advantage to whichever host genotype is currently rare.
Describe the resulting cycle: common genotype → parasite tracks it → rare genotype now favoured → frequencies shift → cycle repeats.
Explain in your own words why no single host genotype stays best forever.
activities.title: Parasite-host cycling with fast generations

feedback: If a learner assumes co-evolution always means predator vs prey, use the orchid-moth match to show mutualists co-evolve too.

If a learner is unsure how a species can be predicted, highlight that a very deep nectar spur implies some pollinator must have a tongue long enough to reach it; tight trait-matching like this can arise when partners drive each other's evolution.
activities.intendedInsight: Co-evolution is not only conflict: in a mutualism each partner shapes the other's traits, producing matched features. A reciprocal relationship can be close enough to let scientists forecast an unknown partner — Darwin's long-tongued hawk moth prediction was later confirmed.
learnerActions: Examine an illustration of an orchid with a long nectar spur and the matching tongue length of its moth pollinator, with Darwin's prediction annotated.
Measure (or read off) the depth of the orchid's nectar spur.
Use the length-matching relationship to 'predict' the tongue length of an unknown moth pollinator, as Darwin did before the moth was found.
Explain why co-evolution can produce such a tight match between two partners that benefit each other.
State how this mutualistic case differs from a predator-prey arms race while still being reciprocal co-evolution.
activities.title: Mutualism and prediction: the orchid and the hawk moth

feedback: If a learner labels climate adaptation as an arms race, point out the environment does not counter-evolve; only a living partner pushes back.

If a learner says a species 'won', remind them that while both partners keep evolving, each gain tends to be matched, so relative fitness stays roughly constant; a lasting 'win' would usually mean the partner stopped keeping up or died out.
If a learner reads 'staying in the same place' as no genetic change, clarify that constant genetic change is needed just to hold the same relative position.
activities.intendedInsight: Co-evolution is RECIPROCAL — each species is part of the other's selection pressure — and is distinct from adapting to a cold or dry environment, which does not evolve back. Antagonistic and mutualistic co-evolution are both reciprocal; while both sides keep evolving, any advantage one side gains tends to be answered, so neither gets permanently ahead (although in real life a species can still lose by going extinct).
learnerActions: Given short scenarios (e.g. a lizard adapting to a colder climate vs a moth evolving against a bat's echolocation), decide which involve a co-evolving partner and which are adaptation to a non-living environment.
Match examples to the labels 'antagonistic arms race', 'mutualistic co-evolution', or 'one-sided adaptation to a fixed environment'.
Answer whether one species can permanently 'win' an arms race, and justify briefly.
Explain the slogan 'running to stay in the same place' in terms of relative fitness against a co-evolving partner.
activities.title: Check: tell co-evolution from one-sided adaptation
